stories.title: LOFAR delivers an ultra-deep sub-arcsecond image of the ELAIS-N1 radio sky
paragraphs: Phys.org reports a Leiden University–led LOFAR team produced what it calls the sharpest and most sensitive low-frequency radio image yet of ELAIS-N1, covering about 25 full-Moon areas of sky and revealing nearly 63,000 radio sources.

In an arXiv preprint accepted for Astronomy & Astrophysics, J.M.G.H.J. de Jong and collaborators present 200 hours of High-Band Antenna data at 115–168 MHz over 2.5×2.5 deg². The highest-resolution mosaic reaches 5.3 μJy beam−1 at 0.33″×0.39″ centrally (area-weighted 7.4 μJy beam−1 at 0.36″×0.45″); combining with prior deep 6″ LOFAR images yields 62,916 unique sources.

According to Phys.org, the image is about 20 times sharper than the previous deepest LOFAR map of this field, contains about 8 billion pixels, and drew on roughly 400 terabytes of data processed on SURF's Spider platform after calibration advances cut costs by more than a factor of 10. The authors release the data publicly for multi-wavelength follow-up and frame it as a benchmark for LOFAR2.0 and SKA-era surveys.

image.credit: De Jong et al., via Phys.org coverage

stories.title: Asteroid shape and aim can change nuclear deflection thrust by up to 5x
paragraphs: Universe Today reports new Icarus research led by Sandia National Laboratories physicist Nathan Moore on stand-off pulsed X-ray deflection of near-Earth objects—detonating a pulsed energy device near an asteroid so surface vaporization provides thrust without relying on a kinetic impactor alone.

According to the paper as summarized by Universe Today, the team built an algorithm more than 1,600 times faster than earlier models so it can include real three-dimensional topography. Demonstrations on Bennu, Itokawa, and Golevka found orientation at intercept can raise deflection velocity by up to nearly 2x, 4x, and 5x respectively versus each body's minimum response.

The authors warn that an incoming NEO's shape and uncontrolled orientation may be unknown, so aim matters strongly, and the current model still cannot accurately predict breakup of the entire asteroid body—only surface rock vaporization and related effects.

stories.title: Hubble's Messier 30 image shows how globular clusters record galactic history
paragraphs: NASA says a new Hubble Space Telescope image of globular cluster Messier 30 (NGC 7099), about 27,500 light-years away in Capricornus, combines ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared data from multiple observing programs spanning more than 15 years.

According to NASA, globular clusters hold tens of thousands to millions of stars, typically orbit in a galaxy's halo, and are estimated at roughly 11.5 to 13.5 billion years old. Historically, Harlow Shapley's cluster distance work showed the Sun is not at the galactic center.

NASA notes researchers have found that M30 and many other clusters orbit opposite the Milky Way's spin, which may mean they were captured rather than formed in place. Repeat Hubble visits track how different stellar populations move and help study blue stragglers and multiple populations inside a single cluster.

image.credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini
image.alt: Hubble image of globular cluster Messier 30

stories.title: Blind listeners and musicians show less internal noise in pitch hearing
paragraphs: In The Conversation, Georgia Tech psychologist Woon Ju Park summarizes a Journal of Neuroscience study comparing nine people blind before age 2 with 18 sighted participants who had varied musical training on tone-in-noise detection and pitch discrimination tasks.

Park writes that early-blind participants outperformed sighted peers only on pitch discrimination, pointing to brain-level processing rather than cochlear frequency selectivity. A mathematical model attributed the advantage to lower internal noise—more consistent responses to the same sound over time.

The same analysis found that musical training similarly reduced internal noise in sighted musicians compared with people who were neither early-blind nor extensively trained. Park says how much training is needed, and whether gains extend to everyday complex listening, remains open.
